summary: For ages 12–13 (GCSE lead-in / NGSS HS placement), this procedural topic covers three linked quantitative skills: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (as a ratio/percentage), constructing and interpreting to-scale Sankey diagrams, and work done = force × distance (joules). All three rest on conservation of energy and dissipation: no real device is 100% efficient, and 'wasted' energy is dissipated (usually to the thermal store of the surroundings), not destroyed. The core activity is a build-and-calculate bench where learners set an input, drag the useful/wasted split, see arrows redraw to scale and an efficiency readout update, plus a work-done tool linking force and distance to W = Fd. Reading-a-Sankey reference, calculation practice, and predict-then-check problems support this.
misconceptions: 'Wasted energy is lost/destroyed' — it is dissipated (spread out, usually to the thermal store of the surroundings), still conserved; the Sankey's wasted arrow accounts for it.
Drawing Sankey arrows not to scale, or with output widths that don't sum to the input — breaking conservation in the representation.
Believing a device can be >100% efficient, or that a more efficient device 'creates' or 'saves' energy rather than wasting less of it.
Thinking 'useful' vs 'wasted' is a fixed property of an energy type rather than depending on the device's purpose.
Work-done errors: counting work when there is no movement (holding still), using the wrong (perpendicular) distance, or conflating work, force and power.

activities.title: Sankey-and-efficiency bench: build energy transfers to scale
steps: Set a device's input energy (e.g. 100 J into a motor).
Drag the split between the useful output branch and the wasted (dissipated) branch; watch the arrow widths redraw to scale in real time.
Read the live efficiency meter showing useful ÷ total as a percentage.
Try to drag the useful arrow wider than the input — notice it cannot exceed the input, and efficiency cannot pass 100%.
Observe the wasted branch labelled 'dissipated to surroundings (thermal)' peeling off rather than vanishing.
Check that the useful and wasted branch widths sum back to the input width every time.
Work predict-then-check problems: predict the efficiency and arrow widths, then set the split and compare.
activities.insight: Efficiency is the fraction of input energy that ends up useful; input = useful + wasted, so efficiency can never exceed 100% and 'wasted' energy is dissipated, not destroyed. Drawing arrow widths in proportion makes conservation visible rather than decorative.

activities.title: Work done = force × distance: make W = Fd a felt quantity
steps: Push an object (e.g. a crate) with a force arrow through a distance; watch W = F × d accumulate with units (N × m = J).
Adjust force and distance (e.g. sliders) and observe how W changes.
Compute a worked case: W = 20 N × 2 m = 40 J, stating units.
Test the 'holding still' case: keep the load stationary and see that zero distance gives zero work, even though holding feels effortful.
Check that the distance used is the distance moved in the direction of the force, not a perpendicular distance.
activities.insight: Work done is energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance in the force's direction; no movement means no work in physics, which contrasts with the everyday sense of 'effort'.

activities.title: Useful vs wasted depends on the device's purpose
steps: Compare two devices: a lamp (whose thermal output is wasted) and a heater (whose thermal output is useful).
For each, label the same type of transfer as useful or wasted according to what the device is for.
State the device's purpose and then decide which output branch of its Sankey is 'useful'.
activities.insight: 'Useful' and 'wasted' are not fixed properties of an energy type — the same thermal output can be useful or wasted depending on what the device is meant to do.

activities.title: Read and interpret a given Sankey diagram
steps: Examine a labelled Sankey diagram (e.g. tap branches to reveal energy values and useful/wasted labels).
Identify which branch is the useful output and which is wasted/dissipated.
Explain why the input arrow's width equals the sum of the output arrows' widths.
Spot the error: given several Sankey diagrams, pick the one that conserves energy and say what is wrong with the others (e.g. outputs that don't sum to the input).
activities.insight: Reading a Sankey means recognising that arrow width represents energy amount, that each branch is useful or wasted, and that total in must equal total out.

activities.title: Consolidate with calculation practice
steps: Calculate efficiency as a percentage from given input and useful output values, placing useful energy over total input.
Solve W = Fd problems for given force and distance, stating units.
Given a Sankey diagram, identify the useful and wasted branches.
Decide 'which Sankey conserves energy?' from a set, justifying the choice by checking the outputs sum to the input.
activities.insight: Fluency with the efficiency ratio and the work formula, and the ability to spot a conservation error in a Sankey, demonstrate the procedural outcomes.

checkQuestion: Here are the figures for a motor: 100 J of electrical energy in, 60 J transferred usefully to lifting. Calculate its efficiency, draw a Sankey diagram to scale for this motor, then use W = Fd to find the work done lifting a 20 N load through 2 m. Talk me through it as you go. [Watch: efficiency = useful/total; wasted 40 J shown branching; arrows proportional and summing to the input; W = 20×2 = 40 J with units.]
checkAnswer: Efficiency = useful/total × 100 = 60/100 = 60%. Sankey: one 100 J input arrow splitting into a 60 J useful arrow (straight on) and a 40 J wasted arrow (branching down, usually to thermal), widths in proportion and summing to the input. Work done = F × d = 20 N × 2 m = 40 J. Throughout, input energy equals useful plus wasted (energy conserved).
